articles.title: Dajaune Brown Celebrates First Goal for Rochdale AFC on Derby Day
articles.excerpt: Dajaune Brown expressed his joy after scoring his first goal for Rochdale AFC during a derby match, describing the experience as a 'terrific feeling'.
articles.content_html:
Dajaune Brown has described scoring his first goal for Rochdale AFC as a 'terrific feeling' following the club's derby match on September 19, 2026. The goal marked a significant milestone for the player, who joined the team earlier this season.

The match saw Rochdale AFC face off against their local rivals, creating an electric atmosphere among fans and players alike. Brown's contribution was pivotal in the team's performance during this highly anticipated fixture.

Brown expressed gratitude towards the supporters for their encouragement throughout the match. Looking ahead, Rochdale AFC will aim to build on this success in their upcoming fixtures.

articles.title: Heights Lane Roadworks Scheduled from 26 October 2026
articles.excerpt: Heights Lane in Rochdale will be temporarily closed for roadworks from 26 October to 1 November 2026, affecting local traffic routes.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Borough Council has announced that Heights Lane will undergo roadworks from Monday, 26 October 2026, to Sunday, 1 November 2026. The work will result in a temporary closure of Heights Lane from its junction with Knowsley Street to its junction with Mizzy Road.

The roadworks will take place daily from 8am to 5pm, which may impact local traffic during these hours. Motorists are advised to use alternative routes, including Howard Street, Whitehall Street, and Quarry Street, to navigate around the closure.

This development is part of ongoing efforts to improve local infrastructure and ensure the safety of road users. Residents and commuters are encouraged to plan their journeys accordingly during this period.

For further information, residents can view a map of roadworks across Greater Manchester on the Rochdale Borough Council website.

articles.title: Rochdale AFC Secures 2-0 Victory Over Oldham Athletic
articles.excerpt: Rochdale AFC moved off the bottom of the League Two table with a 2-0 win against Oldham Athletic in a closely contested Greater Manchester derby on Saturday, September 19, 2026.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale AFC lifted themselves off the bottom of the League Two table with a 2-0 victory against Oldham Athletic in their Greater Manchester derby on Saturday, September 19, 2026. The match, held at the Crown Oil Arena, saw the home side take an early lead just seven minutes into the game.

Charlie Tasker and Jonny Smith combined effectively down the right flank, with Tasker delivering a low cross that was met by Dan Moss, who swept the ball into the roof of the net. Oldham's Mike Fondop had a golden opportunity to equalise in the 25th minute but missed an open goal, sliding the ball wide after a mistake from Rochdale goalkeeper Nils Ramming, who was dispossessed by Keenan Appiah-Forson.

The visitors continued to press for an equaliser after the interval, with Kane Drummond's delivery across the face of goal evading both Fondop and substitute Calum Kavanagh. However, Rochdale struck again in the 62nd minute, doubling their lead when Baba Adeeko headed the ball forward for Dajaune Brown, who advanced into the penalty area, sidestepped defender Donervon Daniels, and fired a powerful shot into the bottom corner.

This victory is significant for Rochdale as it not only boosts their morale but also improves their position in the league standings. The team will look to build on this momentum in their upcoming fixtures as they aim to climb further up the League Two table.

articles.title: Planning Permission Granted for Seven Homes on Former New Jerusalem Church Site in Middleton
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Council has approved plans for seven new family homes on the site of the former New Jerusalem Church on Egerton Street, Middleton, despite objections regarding parking and green space.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Council has granted planning permission for the construction of seven new homes on the site of the former New Jerusalem Church, located on Egerton Street in Middleton. The church, which was established before 1886, was demolished in 2012, leaving the site vacant.

The developer, Zest Eco, proposed the construction of seven three-bedroom townhouses, each featuring private gardens and dedicated parking. The planning documents state that the development aims to meet the identified need for family housing rather than higher-density flat accommodation. The new homes will include rear dormers and solar panels, with access provided via a new dropped kerb from Egerton Street.

Despite the approval, the plans faced five objections from local residents. Concerns included the potential loss of on-street parking for existing residents, fears of overdevelopment, and the loss of green space in the area. The council's planning committee noted these objections but ultimately decided to proceed with the development, citing the benefits of regenerating a brownfield site and providing much-needed family housing.

The development is expected to contribute positively to the local community by enhancing the residential character of the neighbourhood. Construction is likely to commence in the near future, although specific timelines have yet to be confirmed. Residents will be informed of any significant developments regarding the project as it progresses.

The Heywood Community Gala, which took place from 18 to 20 September at The Pig and Whistle, has come under scrutiny after photos from the event showed a significantly smaller setup than the colourful promotional material suggested. The event was advertised as featuring large fairground rides, live music, street food, and children's entertainment, but images released on Saturday morning depicted only a handful of gazebos outside the venue, with no large rides in sight.

The promotional artwork, generated by AI, depicted a vibrant scene with performers, balloons, and crowds, leading to comparisons on social media with Glasgow's infamous Willy Wonka experience, which faced similar criticism in 2024 for not meeting expectations. A Facebook page, Cameron Boland - Scam Event Watch & Awareness, has been vocal in its criticism of the Heywood event, alleging it was a scam and questioning the adequacy of security and entertainment arrangements.

Cameron Boland, the organiser, has been accused of mismanaging previous events, including a similar gala that was cancelled by Salford City Council and Greater Manchester Police in August. While the Facebook page has raised concerns about the gala's setup, including claims that performers were situated on a rug between tables, these allegations have not been independently verified. The photographs from the event do show activity taking place, but they do not provide a complete picture of what was available throughout the three-day event.

Kelly, the tenant and operator of The Pig and Whistle, defended the event, stating that it was still ongoing and that there were activities planned for the remainder of the weekend. The situation has raised questions about the expectations set by promotional materials versus the actual experience provided, highlighting the importance of transparency in event advertising.

articles.title: St Luke’s Church in Deeplish to Host Outdoor Service on September 20
articles.excerpt: St Luke’s Church in Deeplish will host an outdoor service on September 20 at 10.30am, followed by refreshments. A new youth group, Roots, will also start on September 20.
articles.content_html:
St Luke’s Church in Deeplish will hold a service of Morning Praise on Sunday, September 20, at 10.30am, weather permitting. The service will take place in the church car park, providing a relaxed atmosphere for attendees of all ages and backgrounds. Following the service, refreshments including tea, coffee, and cake will be available for those who wish to stay and chat.

Reader Sue Horobin will officiate the Morning Praise service, which aims to welcome both regular members and newcomers to the congregation. The church encourages anyone interested in learning more about its activities to join the service, which has no dress code and is designed to be informal and friendly.

In addition to the outdoor service, St Luke’s Church will also host a Bible study group on Wednesday, September 23, at 10am. This group is open to anyone who wishes to explore the Bible in a welcoming environment. Later that day, another Morning Praise service will be held at 11am, officiated by Revd Natty Gray.

Starting on the same day, September 20, a new youth group called Roots will be launched at St Saviour's Church. This group is aimed at school children in Years 6 to 9 and will run every other Sunday from 4pm to 5.30pm. Participants can expect fun games, activities, and discussions about the Bible with peers. For more information about the youth group or church activities, interested individuals can contact the church office.

articles.title: Kashmir Youth Project Marks Year of Community Achievements in Rochdale
articles.excerpt: The Kashmir Youth Project celebrated a successful year of community engagement, reporting over 11,000 interactions and significant financial gains for local residents during its annual meeting.
articles.content_html:
Members, volunteers, partners, staff and community supporters gathered to celebrate the achievements of the Kashmir Youth Project (KYP) during its annual general and public meetings held on 19 September 2026. The event highlighted the impact KYP has made across Rochdale over the past year, showcasing its commitment to community welfare and support.

Throughout the year 2025/26, KYP recorded 11,259 engagements and visits across its various services, which include advice and welfare, learning and skills, adult day care, and a community food pantry. The organisation collaborated with over 80 agencies, delivering more than 200 community events and activities aimed at strengthening partnerships and creating opportunities for local residents.

KYP's efforts have resulted in significant financial and social value for the community, securing £2 million in financial gains for residents through 3,526 client interventions. These interventions provided essential advice, guidance, and support to those in need, demonstrating the organisation's vital role in the local area.

The expansion of KYP's Advice and Welfare Outreach locations has further enhanced its reach, increasing from five to 11 centres across Rochdale, Heywood, and Middleton. This growth allows KYP to assist more residents in accessing the necessary services and opportunities to improve their lives. Additionally, the organisation delivered 8,460 learning hours and supported 164 individuals in pursuing further training and employment.

articles.title: Are there really fairies in Healey Dell?
articles.excerpt: The rocky cleft known as the Fairies’ Chapel is a real landscape feature with a long history of local storytelling — but the supernatural claims rest in folklore, not in official records.
articles.summary: The rocky cleft known as the Fairies’ Chapel is a real landscape feature with a long history of local storytelling — but the supernatural claims rest in folklore, not in official records.
articles.body:
Healey Dell sits where the River Spodden squeezes through a narrow gorge known locally as the Thrutch, a shady, waterfall‑scattered hollow two miles north of Rochdale town centre. Today it is a council‑managed nature reserve with a heritage centre, tea rooms and family trails; the long stone viaduct that towers above the gorge is a Grade II listed structure and the Dell is promoted as a place of industrial archaeology and wild beauty. ([rochdale.gov.uk](https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/directory-record/737/healey-dell-nature-reserve-and-tea-rooms-rochdale))

The name “Fairies’ Chapel” points to one of the Dell’s most persistent stories: a pocket of hollowed rock that, to Victorian and earlier visitors, looked like a tiny church with a pulpit and seats carved by the water. Local guidebooks and the Healey Dell Heritage Centre explain that the “chapel” is essentially a water‑worn niche in the rock — a natural feature shaped by erosion rather than human carving. That explanation sits alongside the telling that a great summer storm in the 1830s changed the Spodden’s course and altered or buried parts of the formation people once pointed to. ([healeydelltearooms.co.uk](https://www.healeydelltearooms.co.uk/things-to-do/the-fairies-chapel/))

Where the written history stops, folklore gathers. The most often‑repeated version appears in nineteenth‑century collections of Lancashire tales: the Fairies’ Chapel becomes the stage for tricks, warnings and moral tales involving fairies, witches, prophetic “Fairy Queens” and local characters such as millers and gentry. Robert Roby’s Lancashire Legends (a Victorian compilation that survives in full online) gives a long, theatrical account in which a narrow rocky hollow is haunted by “the good people,” encounters with enchanted hares and strange lights, and episodes of bewitchment and retribution. These are literary and oral traditions rather than records of events that can be checked against archives. ([upload.wikimedia.org](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/c/c1/Lancashire_legends_%28IA_lancashirelegend00roby%29.pdf))

Later local retellings and the Dell’s own heritage material mix Roby’s account with other regional motifs: witches turned to stone by a Fairy King, a fortune‑teller called Mother Bagden, and love stories involving the Byron and Chadwick families. These stories are clearly labelled as legend by the heritage centre and by council information aimed at visitors; they help explain why the spot became one of the Dell’s most evocative attractions, but they are not supported by contemporary documentary evidence of supernatural events. ([healeydelltearooms.co.uk](https://www.healeydelltearooms.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/history/Fairies-Chapel-final.pdf))

That distinction matters. The documented facts are straightforward: Healey Dell is an historically important landscape (with a listed viaduct and remnants of mills) and it is managed as a local nature reserve. The physical rock features people called the Fairies’ Chapel are the result of ordinary geological and fluvial action; floods and industrial change have altered the appearance of the Dell since at least the early nineteenth century. Claims that fairies, witches or a Fairy King literally created or inhabit the chapel are part of oral tradition and folklore — rich, culturally valuable stories, but not verifiable historical fact. ([historicengland.org.uk](https://historicengland.org.uk/listing/the-list/list-entry/1317784))

If you come looking for fairies, the sensible local advice is to bring imagination and respect. The Dell’s folklore is part of what makes it special: the stories connect people across generations to place and to the Dell’s industrial and natural past. If you want the clearest separation between what’s recorded and what’s told, read the nineteenth‑century legends as folklore, and the council and heritage centre material as the place’s recorded history and practical visitor information. ([upload.wikimedia.org](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/c/c1/Lancashire_legends_%28IA_lancashirelegend00roby%29.pdf))

Bottom line: there is nothing in the official record to confirm supernatural activity at the Fairies’ Chapel — only enduring, well‑documented local stories that have been collected, retold and celebrated by authors and by the Healey Dell community. The chapel is best enjoyed as a meeting point of geology, industrial archaeology and imagination — a small landscape where the boundary between history and legend is part of the attraction. ([rochdale.gov.uk](https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/directory-record/737/healey-dell-nature-reserve-and-tea-rooms-rochdale))

articles.title: Ignite Fire Festival Returns to Rochdale with New Displays from November 20-22, 2026
articles.excerpt: The Ignite Fire Festival will illuminate Rochdale Town Hall square with new attractions from November 20-22, 2026, featuring fire sculptures, music, and community performances.
articles.content_html:
The Ignite Fire Festival is set to return to Rochdale Town Hall square from Friday, November 20 to Sunday, November 22, 2026. This year’s festival promises to be bigger and better, featuring brand-new displays and attractions that will transform the area into a magical spectacle of fire, lights, and sound.

Organised by Rochdale Development Agency, the free event will include immersive trails and spectacular fire sculptures. Last year, the festival attracted over 10,000 visitors, and this year, attendees can expect to walk through blazing installations created by the award-winning outdoor arts specialists Walk the Plank. The festival will also showcase community arts, including a performance titled 'Fireflies', which involves local residents trained in fire-spinning.

Councillor Sue Smith, cabinet member for communities and co-operation at Rochdale Borough Council, expressed enthusiasm for the festival, stating that it has quickly become one of the most popular events in the borough. She encouraged families to mark their calendars for what promises to be an exciting winter experience leading up to the Christmas lights switch-on, which will take place on the final evening of the festival.

The Ignite Fire Festival is funded by Rochdale Borough Council, the Greater Manchester Combined Authority's Flexible Fund, and in partnership with Walk the Plank and Culture Co-op. Further details about the festival will be available next month on the Rochdale Council website.

articles.title: Rochdale MP Paul Waugh Highlights Local Achievements as Minister for Early Education
articles.excerpt: Paul Waugh, Rochdale's MP, reflects on his new role as Minister for Early Education and its impact on local initiatives, including the Holiday Activities and Food programme and the £20m Pride in Place fund.
articles.content_html:
Paul Waugh, the Member of Parliament for Rochdale, has shared insights into his recent appointment as Minister for Early Education and its significance for the local community. In an article published on 18 September 2026, Waugh expressed pride in representing Rochdale at a governmental level, a milestone he described as a historic change for the town, which had not seen a local MP hold a ministerial position for nearly two centuries.

During the summer, Waugh visited various local organisations, including KYP, BACP, and Aspire 2 Inspire, where he observed the positive impact of the Government's Holiday Activities and Food programme. This initiative aims to provide children with nutritious meals and engaging activities during school holidays, a crucial support for families in the area. Waugh emphasised the importance of such programmes in ensuring that children receive a proper start in life, reflecting his commitment to enhancing educational opportunities in Rochdale.

Waugh also highlighted the Best Start Family Hub on Derby Street in Heywood, one of seventeen hubs across the borough that support families from pregnancy through early childhood. He noted that this support is vital for local families and pledged to advocate for its expansion. Additionally, he mentioned the £20 million Pride in Place fund allocated to Smallbridge, Hurstead, and Belfield, which aims to empower local residents to shape their community's future. Waugh has been actively engaging with residents to understand their needs and priorities for this funding.

Looking ahead, Waugh is set to represent the UK at UNESCO's Digital Learning Week in Paris, where he will discuss the integration of artificial intelligence in education. He remains committed to ensuring that local voices are heard in government decisions and that Rochdale continues to thrive under his ministerial role.

articles.title: Traffic Calming Measures Approved for Grimshaw Lane in Middleton
articles.excerpt: Middleton Township Committee has approved a traffic order to enhance safety on Grimshaw Lane, introducing pedestrian crossing islands and reducing on-street parking following concerns over speeding and accidents.
articles.content_html:
Middleton Township Committee has approved a traffic order aimed at improving safety on Grimshaw Lane, a road described as "dangerous" due to a history of speeding and serious accidents, including a fatality. The decision was made during a meeting on September 17, 2026, where the committee greenlit the introduction of three pedestrian crossing islands, the extension of bus stops, and a reduction in on-street parking.

Councillor Dylan Williams, who represents the area and serves as the Rochdale Council portfolio holder for highways and facilities, stated that the initiative has been in the works for four-and-a-half years. He noted that the road layout has been identified as a significant factor contributing to the number of road traffic accidents (RTAs), and the new measures are designed to address these issues. The changes will also include narrowing parts of the road and improving access for disabled individuals at junctions with Shawbury Street, Sedgley Street, and Sandy Lane.

The traffic order was prompted by objections from 11 residents, primarily concerned about the potential loss of parking outside their homes. Despite the objections, Williams reported that the majority of residents consulted were supportive of the proposed changes. The meeting reportedly became heated, reflecting the strong feelings surrounding the parking issue.

The implementation of these traffic calming measures is expected to enhance safety for pedestrians and drivers alike, potentially reducing the risk of further accidents on Grimshaw Lane. The council will now proceed with the necessary arrangements to put the approved measures into effect.

Greater Manchester Police are investigating a series of social media posts in which young people threatened each other with violence, including the use of knives and other weapons. This investigation follows a recent stabbing incident in Rochdale town centre, where a 15-year-old boy sustained serious injuries.

PC Jake Peverley, who is handling some of these cases, acknowledged the understandable concern within the community following the stabbing. He stated, "Incidents such as this have a significant impact on young people, families and the wider community."

The police have reassured residents that all reports of threats are being taken seriously and are under thorough investigation. They emphasised that threats of violence, whether made online or in person, can lead to fear and distress and may constitute criminal offences.

Residents are encouraged to remain vigilant and report any concerning behaviour. The police are committed to ensuring the safety of the community and addressing any threats that arise.
